1. Validate the current bill: confirm meter reads imply 787 kWh (62,473 − 61,686) and that line items sum to $147.84; confirm last month’s $156.44, so the observed change is −$8.60. Any arithmetic mismatch becomes a suspected billing error.

2. Map each billing period to the OpenEI tariff by date: last month (2026-02-24 to 2026-03-26) falls entirely under the pre-2026-04-10 tariff (fixed $18.38; variable $0.0263125 + $0.13441 = $0.1607225/kWh for the first 2,000 kWh). The current period (2026-03-26 to 2026-04-25) straddles the 2026-04-10 change, so prorate the fixed charge ($18.38 vs $18.788) and blend the variable rate ($0.1607225 vs $0.0347738 + $0.13299 = $0.1677638/kWh) across the boundary.

3. Set days_usd = 0 because both periods are 30 days.

4. Estimate weather_usd from the NOAA history: compare last month (2.5 CDD / 549.5 HDD) to the current period (57 CDD / 226 HDD), derive a weather-to-kWh coefficient from the bill history, convert the weather-driven kWh difference to dollars at the effective rate, or set weather_usd = 0 if no defensible coefficient can be estimated.

5. Compute price_usd from the tariff changes (higher fixed charge and higher blended variable rate) applied to baseline usage; compute usage_usd from the 72 kWh decrease (859 → 787) valued at the effective rate; use usage_usd as the residual so price_usd + days_usd + weather_usd + usage_usd equals exactly −$8.60.

6. Check for a billing error by comparing the tariff-modeled current-period total to the actual $147.84; if the difference exceeds rounding, set billing_error_suspected = true and billing_error_usd to the discrepancy, otherwise false and null.

7. Return only the JSON object with keys price_usd, days_usd, weather_usd, usage_usd, billing_error_suspected, and billing_error_usd.
